subject: preparedness-v2

object.value: Whether Version 2’s governance arrangements permit OpenAI Leadership to deploy High-capability models without sufficient safeguards

statement: Preparedness Framework v2’s governance arrangements permit OpenAI Leadership to deploy models with High capabilities without safeguards that sufficiently minimize their associated risks.

time.note: Dated by the edition. OpenAI’s announcement was published with it on 2025-04-15 and the ChatGPT agent system card on 2025-07-17; Coggins et al. submitted v1 of their analysis on 2025-09-29 and revised it as v2 on 2025-10-13.

qualification: Contested assessment of the policy’s permissiveness, not a finding that OpenAI deployed a model without safeguards, a legal ruling or a guarantee of compliance. Coggins et al. (arXiv:2509.24394; v1 2025-09-29, v2 2025-10-13) read the framework’s governance arrangements as letting OpenAI Leadership, the CEO or a person designated by them, approve or reject the Safety Advisory Group’s recommendations and so deploy even more dangerous capabilities, especially if other developers do so. OpenAI’s announcement of Version 2 states that covered systems reaching High capability must have safeguards that sufficiently minimize the associated risk of severe harm before they are deployed, and its ChatGPT agent system card describes the framework as committing it to such safeguards; both predate the analysis and are not replies to it. The record does not decide whether leadership’s authority over the recommendations defeats that stated requirement. The paper’s framework-wide conclusion and OpenAI’s comparison of Version 2 with its predecessor are context. The rule’s own wording is recorded in the provision record for Version 2.

subject: anthropic

object.value: Whether Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust is independent enough of stockholders to exercise effective public-interest oversight of Anthropic in practice

statement: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust has sufficient independence from stockholders to exercise effective public-interest oversight of Anthropic in practice.

time.note: The question is not tied to one date: it concerns the Trust under the rights recorded on this page, which phase in from 6 September 2023. The cited passages were published from 19 September 2023 to 23 July 2026 (the Transparency Hub version last updated that day); those are source dates, not the period of the question.

qualification: The unresolved question is whether the Trust can exercise effective public-interest oversight when stockholder preferences conflict with that oversight. Anthropic describes financially disinterested Trustees, an intended independent design and a checking role; its Transparency Hub says the Trust’s authority to elect directors helps insulate the mission from short-term commercial and shareholder pressures, and its April 2026 announcement says Trust-appointed directors then formed a board majority. Appointment power is distinct from independence against removal. Stein-Perlman’s 2024 analysis tentatively identifies possible stockholder subordination under incompletely disclosed failsafe terms. Fried and Reiter describe partial investor insulation and favour constraints on guardian overreach; they do not simply deny an effective checking role. Outside counsel describe the arrangement’s accountability and amendment mechanisms. Source dates and subsequent phase-in must be distinguished. The inspected public descriptions do not settle practical effectiveness; no side or legal conclusion is adopted.

subject: openai-group-pbc

object.value: Whether the OpenAI Foundation can exercise effective mission-directed control over OpenAI Group PBC in practice after the October 2025 recapitalization

statement: Following the October 2025 recapitalization, the OpenAI Foundation can exercise effective mission-directed control over OpenAI Group PBC in practice.

time.note: Dated by the recapitalization whose control arrangements the question concerns (the certificate filed and the Delaware Attorney General’s letter of 28 October 2025). The date does not bound a period of effective control, and no end is recorded. The cited passages were published from 28 October 2025 to 11 May 2026 (OpenAI’s structure page is undated); those are source dates, not the period of the question.

qualification: Effective control here concerns the Foundation’s ability to enforce its mission through its retained governance powers when commercial interests or Group management resist. OpenAI asserts continuing control; formal rights are documented separately. Bret Taylor’s announcement for OpenAI’s board says the recapitalization keeps the mission at the center and maintains the strongest representation of mission-focused governance in the industry. Not For Private Gain recognises improvements over the abandoned proposal while judging control weaker than under the former structure and identifying conditional risks to effective exercise. CalMatters reports critics’ concerns about possible commercial predominance. Fried and Reiter describe the Foundation’s appointment, veto and safety-blocking powers as substantial authority over investors and argue that guardians may do too much as well as too little. The Delaware Attorney General’s non-objection is conditional on representations. These sources do not settle practical effectiveness, and no legal conclusion or side is adopted.

statement: Trammell and Korinek, “Economic Growth under Transformative AI” (2023-10) articulates E01. Citing the high capital share in AI R&D (Besiroglu et al., 2024), the authors describe a feedback in which automating AI R&D speeds AI capability growth, then cite calibrated models of this feedback (Erdil et al. 2025; Lifland et al. 2025) as having 'speculative elements'. In the risk subsection, the authors contrast a scenario of acceleration from R&D automation alone with scenarios of automated physical production, each with distinct safety concerns.

'Self-improve' is the authors' gloss on automated R&D in growth models, where the improved object is general technology; the claim is about growth, and the abstract says R&D automation alone may not produce the transformation. (Second passage) Wording checked against the April 2026 revision of NBER w31815 (first issued October 2023); whether this wording appears in the October 2023 version was not checked, so it is attested only from April 2026. The passage cites 2024–2025 work, so this wording is not in the October 2023 version. 'In some sense' hedges the claim; the predictions of near-complete R&D automation are attributed to the cited models, not asserted by the authors. statement: Trammell and Korinek, “Economic Growth under Transformative AI (October 2023 version)” (2023-10) articulates E05. time.note: The date printed on the cover of the file inspected. It is not stated to be the date on which the file was first posted; the library entry gives 18 July 2025 as the publication date.

qualification: Records the dated file inspected. The library entry was last updated on 20 April 2026 and gives a publication date of 18 July 2025. Whether the November text differs from the draft content approved in July 2025 was not compared, so provisions are dated by the November file only.

subject: eu-gpai-guidelines-2025

object.value: Providers outside an adequately assessed code are expected to show compliance by other adequate means and report to the AI Office

statement: The guidelines state that providers that do not adhere to an adequately assessed code of practice are expected to demonstrate how they comply with Chapter V of the AI Act by other adequate means, and that they may face a larger number of requests for information and for access to conduct model evaluations.

time.note: Provision as stated in the guidelines file dated Brussels 19.11.2025 (C(2025) 7719 final). The Commission’s library entry gives a publication date of 18 July 2025; the July text was not compared.

qualification: The Commission’s stated expectation. The second part is introduced with “may” and gives the reason that the AI Office would have less understanding of such providers’ compliance. No provider is named and no request is recorded. It states what the text provides, not whether any named developer falls within it or complies. A document’s statement is not evidence of implementation, compliance or enforcement.

subject: eu-gpai-guidelines-2025

object.value: Guidelines are not binding; the CJEU gives authoritative interpretation; the Commission bases enforcement on them

statement: The guidelines state that they are not binding for providers of general-purpose AI models, that an authoritative interpretation of the AI Act may only be given by the Court of Justice of the European Union, and that they set out the Commission’s interpretation and application of the AI Act, on which it will base its enforcement action.

time.note: Provision as stated in the guidelines file dated Brussels 19.11.2025 (C(2025) 7719 final). The Commission’s library entry gives a publication date of 18 July 2025; the July text was not compared.

qualification: A statement about the status of the guidelines, in the guidelines themselves. It states what the text provides, not whether any named developer falls within it or complies. A document’s statement is not evidence of implementation, compliance or enforcement.

parties.actor: Court of Justice of the European Union (authoritative interpretation of the AI Act)

subject: eu-gpai-training-summary-template-2025

object.value: Summary updated when further training on additional data requires it, at six-month intervals or sooner

statement: The Explanatory Notice states that the public summary of training content should be updated whenever the provider further trains its model on additional data that requires an update of its content, at six-month intervals or sooner if the additional data requires a materially significant update.

time.note: Provision as stated in the file dated Brussels 5.12.2025 (C(2025) 8311 final). The library entry gives a publication date of 24 July 2025; the July text was not compared.

qualification: Paragraph (29) of the Explanatory Notice. The PDF misspells "intervals" as "intervanls"; the paraphrase corrects the spelling. The Notice also states that summaries of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 are due by 2 August 2027; that sentence is not recorded here. It states what the text provides, not whether any named developer falls within it or complies. A document’s statement is not evidence of implementation, compliance or enforcement.

subject: eu-gpai-training-summary-template-2025

object.value: Template asks for the top 10% of crawled domain names by content size (top 5% or 1,000 for SMEs)

statement: The Template for the public summary of training content asks providers, where content from internet domains was crawled or scraped for training, to list the domain names in the top 10% of all domain names by size of content scraped, and asks small and medium-sized enterprises, including start-ups, to disclose the top 5% of domain names or 1,000 domain names, whichever is lower.

time.note: Provision as stated in the file dated Brussels 5.12.2025 (C(2025) 8311 final). The library entry gives a publication date of 24 July 2025; the July text was not compared.

qualification: Section 2.3 of the Template as it appears in the Communication. The obligation to publish a summary comes from Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act. No summary published by any provider was inspected. It states what the text provides, not whether any named developer falls within it or complies. A document’s statement is not evidence of implementation, compliance or enforcement.

subject: new-york-raise-act-chapter-96-2026

object.value: Civil penalty up to $1,000,000 for a first violation and $3,000,000 per subsequent violation

statement: Section 1427(1) of the General Business Law, as added by the bill, provides that the attorney general may bring a civil action to recover a civil penalty of up to one million dollars for a first violation and up to three million dollars per subsequent violation, determined based on the severity of the violation, where a large frontier developer fails to publish or transmit a compliant required document, makes a prohibited statement, fails to report an incident as required, or fails to comply with its own frontier AI framework.

time.note: Provision as printed in S8828, signed as Chapter 96 on 2026-03-27; effective 2027-01-01.

qualification: A ceiling and a power, not a record of any penalty. The bill also states that it creates no private right of action. It states what the text provides, not whether any named developer falls within it or complies. A document’s statement is not evidence of implementation, compliance or enforcement.

subject: new-york-raise-act-chapter-96-2026

object.value: A large frontier developer must write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework

statement: Section 1421(1) of the General Business Law, as added by the bill, provides that a large frontier developer shall write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on its website a frontier AI framework that applies to its frontier models and describes in detail how it handles the listed subjects, including thresholds for catastrophic risk, mitigations, third-party assessment and critical safety incidents.

time.note: Provision as printed in S8828, signed as Chapter 96 on 2026-03-27; effective 2027-01-01.

A document’s statement is not evidence of implementation, compliance or enforcement.

subject: new-york-raise-act-chapter-96-2026

time.note: Provision as published in the Official Journal on 2026-07-24 (the Regulation is dated 8 July 2026); the Regulation enters into force on 2026-07-27.

qualification: These dates concern high-risk AI systems, not the obligations of general-purpose AI model providers in Chapter V. The same point (40) replaces point (a) and adds point (d); the inspected amending text contains no amendment of point (b), the Chapter V date. This record shows that the AI Act’s dates were amended in 2026 and which dates changed; it does not show that Chapter V dates are unchanged beyond the inspected amending text.

subject: eu-digital-omnibus-ai-2026

object.value: The Commission assesses whether codes of practice cover Articles 53 and 55

statement: Article 1, point (21), of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaces Article 56(6) of the AI Act so that the Commission, taking utmost account of the opinion of the Board, assesses whether the codes of practice cover the obligations in Articles 53 and 55, and publishes its assessment of their adequacy.

time.note: Provision as published in the Official Journal on 2026-07-24 (the Regulation is dated 8 July 2026); the Regulation enters into force on 2026-07-27.

qualification: The amending text. The replaced paragraph in the 2024 text gave the assessment to the AI Office and the Board (separate record). The AI Office is a function of the Commission, and the 2024 Article 3 states that references to the AI Office are construed as references to the Commission. The amendment also removes, in the inspected text of the new paragraph, the sentence on approving a code by implementing act. The recital quoted as context describes codes as having limited legal effect and not granting a presumption of conformity; it is a recital, not an operative provision, and Selekoa does not resolve how it relates to Articles 53(4) and 55(2). Recording an amendment is not evidence that any code was assessed under it.

subject: eu-digital-omnibus-ai-2026

object.value: AI Office exclusively competent for AI systems built on a general-purpose AI model by the same provider

statement: Article 1, point (31), of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaces Article 75(1) of the AI Act so that the AI Office is exclusively competent for supervising and enforcing the Regulation’s obligations for the AI systems it lists, which include AI systems based on general-purpose AI models where the model and the system are developed by the same provider or by providers in the same undertaking, subject to listed exceptions.

time.note: Provision as published in the Official Journal on 2026-07-24 (the Regulation is dated 8 July 2026); the Regulation enters into force on 2026-07-27.

qualification: The amended paragraph concerns AI systems, not general-purpose AI models. The listed exceptions (including systems tied to Annex I products and certain Annex III uses) and the further competence in point (b) for systems that are or are integrated into very large online platforms or search engines are not summarised here. The paragraph extends the competence to the providers of those systems, and to deployers only when they are also the provider or in the same undertaking. It also adds supervisory and enforcement powers in new Articles 75a onwards, which are not recorded. A competence provision is not evidence of any supervision or enforcement action.

parties.actor: AI Office (exclusive competence for supervision and enforcement)

subject: european-parliament-and-council
statement: The European Parliament and the Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, which amends Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and is dated 8 July 2026; it was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026.

time.note: The act is dated at Strasbourg on 8 July 2026 (day precision). The Official Journal publication date is 24 July 2026 and it enters into force on the third day after publication.

qualification: Adoption establishes the text and its date. It does not show how any amended provision is applied. This record covers only the amendments that bear on general-purpose AI model providers and the AI Act’s dates; the Regulation also amends Regulations (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 and many provisions on high-risk AI systems, which are not recorded.

subject: eu-digital-omnibus-ai-2026

object.value: Enters into force on the third day following publication

statement: Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 provides that it enters into force on the third day following its publication in the Official Journal. The Official Journal gives 24 July 2026 as the publication date, which makes the third day 27 July 2026.

time.note: Provision as published in the Official Journal on 2026-07-24 (the Regulation is dated 8 July 2026); the Regulation enters into force on 2026-07-27.

qualification: The date 27 July 2026 is computed from the publication date and is consistent with new Article 113(d) in the Regulation, which says Articles 102 to 110 of the AI Act apply from 27 July 2026. Entry into force of the amending act is not the date of application of every amended provision. The Regulation’s own recital gives urgency before the general application of the AI Act as the reason.

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Class N stock’s director-election rights while held by OpenAI Foundation

statement: The certificate states that, so long as Class N Common Stock is issued, outstanding and held directly or indirectly by OpenAI Foundation, holders of Class A Common Stock may not vote in director elections. Where Class B Common Stock is also outstanding, the Class N shares carry the greater of 66.67% of the voting power or the share of Class N and Class B stock that the Foundation’s Class N shares represent, and no director-election quorum exists without the Class N holder.

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

qualification: What the filed text says. The certificate authorises one share of Class N Common Stock (Section IV.1(a)). The provision conditions its effect on the Foundation’s holding; who actually holds the share is stated by OpenAI (see the record of the Foundation’s right to elect the board), not by this provision.

parties.actor: Holder of the Class N Common Stock (OpenAI Foundation)

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Class N holder’s prior written approval for five kinds of action

statement: The certificate states that, so long as Class N Common Stock is issued, outstanding and held by OpenAI Foundation, the prior written approval of its holder is required for the corporation to amend Article III (Public Benefit); to agree to or complete a deemed liquidation event or a sale of material assets of the corporation and its subsidiaries taken as a whole; to issue more Class N stock; to create or issue other stock entitled to vote on directors, except Class B stock in acquisitions; or to modify the certificate or bylaws in a way that disproportionately and adversely affects the Class N holder.

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

qualification: What the filed text says. The Delaware Attorney General’s statement records OpenAI’s representation of the same approval rights plus a sixth, over amendments to the PBC’s Corporate Governance Guidelines, “as further described in definitive documents”, which were not inspected (context below).

parties.actor: Holder of the Class N Common Stock

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

qualification: What the filed text says. The same section provides that vacancies are filled by a majority vote of the stock entitled to vote on director elections, which it describes as initially controlled by the holder of the Class N stock.

parties.actor: Holder of the Class N Common Stock
Holders of two-thirds of the voting power excluding Class N (at most one-third of the board in twelve months)

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Board considers only the Mission on safety and security issues

statement: OpenAI Group PBC’s certificate of incorporation, filed on 28 October 2025, states that its board of directors must solely consider the Mission, and may not consider the pecuniary interests of stockholders or any other interest, in respect of safety and security issues related to the OpenAI enterprise, including all actions and decisions of the board, its members and its committees.

qualification: What the filed text says, not how the board acts. The Delaware Attorney General’s statement records OpenAI’s representation that the charter provision also covers the actions of the nonprofit board’s Safety and Security Committee; the filed text refers to the PBC’s own board and committees. Whether the two differ in legal effect needs interpretation and is set aside.

subject: rsp-v3-0
statement: Whether RSP v3.0’s new roadmap and transparency mechanisms compensate for its reduced unilateral commitments, in the policy’s overall capacity to secure risk mitigation, remains unsettled.

time.note: v3.0’s effective date; the assessments were published on and after that date.

qualification: Unresolved open question, not a finding; it keeps the strength of the commitments apart from their expected effectiveness. Both sides accept the main changes: v3.0 drops the implied unilateral commitment to pause development and deployment when required safeguards cannot be met, separates recommendations for the industry from what Anthropic commits to as a company, adds transparency commitments, and introduces roadmap goals that are public goals rather than hard commitments. TIME’s report judges that overall the change leaves Anthropic far less constrained by its own safety policies. Sophie Williams and Jonas Freund, writing on GovAI’s site in a post that represents their own views, judge that it weakened future security commitments, note that existing mitigations are not lowered and conclude on balance that honesty about constraints is better than commitments that would not be followed; their article was updated on 2026-03-17 on competitor-matching commitments, and the quoted passages are unchanged. Anthropic describes the revision as amplifying what worked and committing it to more transparency. Holden Karnofsky, who led the revision and writes in his own name, expects more specific and realistic goals to improve their forcing function despite weaker consequences for missing them, and leaves the net effect uncertain. Jared Kaplan, Anthropic’s chief science officer, told TIME that unilateral commitments made no sense while competitors pressed ahead, and denied that the change was a U-turn or a capitulation to market incentives. METR’s Chris Painter, who reviewed an early draft with Anthropic’s permission, called the change understandable but was concerned it might enable a gradual “frog-boiling” effect. None of these passages settles whether the new mechanisms compensate, so all are context. The textual changes are recorded separately, and the record does not decide the question.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Anonymous internal disclosure process with monthly status updates to the discloser and at-least-quarterly sharing with officers and directors

statement: SB 53 requires a large frontier developer to provide a reasonable internal process through which a covered employee may anonymously disclose information the employee believes in good faith shows a specific and substantial danger to public health or safety resulting from a catastrophic risk, or a violation of the Act (Bus. & Prof. Code ch. 25.1). The process must give the discloser a monthly update on the investigation and actions taken, and disclosures and responses must be shared with the developer's officers and directors at least quarterly, except an officer or director whose wrongdoing is alleged.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. This is a statutory requirement only. It is not evidence that any developer has set up or operates such a process. 'Covered employee' has a narrow definition: an employee responsible for assessing, managing, or addressing risk of critical safety incidents (Lab. Code § 1107(b)). The provision therefore does not cover all employees. The applicability of the separate Lab. Code § 1102.5 protections to other employees is not addressed here. Framework texts that describe similar internal reporting channels are not evidence that they respond to this provision unless they say so explicitly.

object.value: Civil penalties under § 22757.15 recoverable only in a civil action brought by the Attorney General

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29; the Governor approved it and it was filed with the Secretary of State that day. qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. The Attorney General-only rule is limited to penalties described in § 22757.15. On the grounds listed in § 22757.15(a), that section makes a large frontier developer subject to a civil penalty whose amount depends on the severity of the violation and does not exceed $1,000,000 per violation. Code § 1107.1(f)–(i), added by the same act, separately refers to civil actions and administrative proceedings 'brought pursuant to this section'. It authorises attorney's fees for a plaintiff who brings a successful action (f), sets a burden-of-proof rule (g), lets a covered employee petition the superior court for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief (h), and bars a stay of that relief pending appeal (i). Who may bring such actions is not resolved here (see stops). No enforcement action is recorded.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Catastrophic risk: death of or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage or loss, from a single incident

statement: SB 53 defines 'catastrophic risk' as a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer's development, storage, use or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or to more than $1 billion in damage to, or loss of, property, arising from a single incident in which a frontier model (a) provides expert-level assistance in creating or releasing a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon; (b) engages without meaningful human oversight in a cyberattack or in conduct that would be murder, assault, extortion or theft if committed by a human; or (c) evades the control of its developer or user. Stated exclusions apply.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Loss of equity value does not count as damage to or loss of property (§ 22757.16). Lab. Code § 1107(a) uses a parallel definition, framed around foundation models, in the whistleblower chapter. This record states the definition only and makes no claim about any model's risk.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Critical safety incident report to OES within 15 days of discovery

statement: SB 53 requires a frontier developer to report any critical safety incident involving one or more of its frontier models to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days of discovering it.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29. Effective 2026-01-01 according to the codified section's history note, 'Effective January 1, 2026' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22757.13, checked 2026-10-04), which shows no amendment. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. § 22757.13(c)(1) is expressly 'subject to paragraph (2)', the 24-hour imminent-risk disclosure (separate record). How the two duties relate is a question of legal interpretation and is not recorded here. Under § 22757.13(h)–(i), OES may adopt regulations designating federal laws, regulations or guidance documents whose incident-reporting standards are substantially equivalent to, or stricter than, this section's. A frontier developer that declares to OES its intent to comply through such a designated standard is deemed in compliance with § 22757.13 to the extent it meets that standard (separate record). Reporting critical safety incidents involving foundation models that are not frontier models is encouraged, not required (§ 22757.13(c)(4)). Critical safety incident reports submitted to OES under § 22757.13 are exempt from the California Public Records Act (§ 22757.13(f)). Beginning 1 January 2027, and annually thereafter, OES must produce a report with anonymised, aggregated information about the critical safety incidents it has reviewed. statement: SB 53 prohibits a large frontier developer from making a materially false or misleading statement about its implementation of, or compliance with, its frontier AI framework. The prohibition does not apply to a statement made in good faith that was reasonable under the circumstances.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. Subdivision (e)(1)(B) concerns statements about a large frontier developer's implementation of, or compliance with, its own frontier AI framework. Subdivision (e)(1)(A) concerns statements by any frontier developer about catastrophic risk from its frontier models or its management of catastrophic risk. Two questions are listed as stops and not resolved here because they need legal interpretation. The first is whether subdivision (e) reaches any named developer's published statement, for example the sentence asserting TFAIA compliance in xAI's December 2025 FAIF (recorded separately as absent from the June 2026 edition). The second is whether that developer is a large frontier developer. A statement in violation of subdivision (e) is one of the grounds on which § 22757.15(a) makes a large frontier developer subject to a civil penalty. This record states what the statute requires. It says nothing about any developer's compliance.

By their text, the following provisions are addressed to frontier developers: the basic transparency report (§ 22757.12(c)(1)); the bar on materially false or misleading statements about catastrophic risk (§ 22757.12(e)(1)(A)); critical-safety-incident reporting (§ 22757.13(c)); and the whistleblower prohibitions and notice duty (Lab. Code § 1107.1(a), (b) and (d)).

The following are addressed only to large frontier developers: the frontier AI framework (§ 22757.12(a)–(b)); the catastrophic-risk summaries in the transparency report (§ 22757.12(c)(2)); internal-use assessment summaries to the Office of Emergency Services (§ 22757.12(d)); the bar on false statements about framework implementation or compliance (§ 22757.12(e)(1)(B)); and the anonymous internal disclosure process (Lab. Code § 1107.1(e)).

The civil-penalty provision (§ 22757.15(a)) names only large frontier developers. This record does not interpret enforcement or applicability beyond the text.

statement: SB 53 requires a frontier developer, before or at the same time as deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, to publish clearly and conspicuously on its website a transparency report with listed basic information. A large frontier developer must also include summaries of its catastrophic-risk assessments under its frontier AI framework, their results, the extent of third-party evaluator involvement, and other steps taken to fulfil its framework for that model.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29 (approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State that day). Effective 2026-01-01 according to the codified section's history note, 'Effective January 1, 2026' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22757.12, checked 2026-10-04). The chaptered bill text itself states no effective date.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. 'Deploy' means making a frontier model available to a third party for use, modification, copying or combination with other software. It excludes making the model available to a third party for the primary purpose of developing or evaluating it (§ 22757.11(e)). The statute does not define 'substantially modified'. A large frontier developer's framework must describe how it decides when its models are substantially modified enough to require these disclosures (§ 22757.12(a)(6)). Publishing the information as part of a larger document, including a system card or model card, is deemed compliance with the applicable paragraph (§ 22757.12(c)(3)). A frontier developer is encouraged, but not required, to make these disclosures consistent with, or superior to, industry best practices (§ 22757.12(c)(4)). Published documents may be redacted where necessary to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety or US national security, or to comply with federal or state law. The developer must describe the character and justification of each redaction, to the extent those concerns permit, and keep the unredacted information for five years (§ 22757.12(f)). A statutory requirement is not evidence that any report was published, or that any report was complete or adequate.

Code § 1107.1, which listed no amendment when checked on 2026-10-04.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. A 'covered employee' is an employee responsible for assessing, managing or addressing risk of critical safety incidents (Lab. Code § 1107(b)). In this chapter 'catastrophic risk' carries the Labor Code definition in § 1107(a). Frontier developers must also give covered employees clear notice of their rights and responsibilities under the section (§ 1107.1(d)). No case or disclosure is recorded.

time.note: Year of the book, as given by its copyright notice; an October 1986 review is recorded in Moravec’s bibliography.

qualification: The compounding runs through molecular manufacturing and new, faster AI systems, and the rise described is of technological advance generally. The wording is attested from 1997.

attested.note: Wording checked in the Foresight Institute’s web edition (© 1986 K. Eric Drexler; published for the web by Russell Whitaker), whose earliest captures are of 1997-07-09; a reader’s message of October 1996 on the site shows the edition was online by then. Not compared with the 1986 printing.

thought.qualifier: Through automated engineering and molecular manufacturing.

subject: drexler-1995-future-forecasts
statement: Drexler’s 1995 forecast comment argues that better computational and material tools accelerate further tool improvement, that a slow trickle of progress seems unlikely, and that computation and molecular machinery could reinforce each other while competing with other technologies.

time.note: Printed footers: 2nd–3rd Quarter 1995.

qualification: Drexler rejects a strict mathematical singularity and calls a reliable schedule impossible, while calling Vinge’s term remarkably appropriate.

thought.missing: Computational and material tools accelerate each other; machine intelligence’s own design ability is not the driver.

subject: eder-1994-re-the-singularity
statement: Eder’s 1994 message describes a positive feedback between technology, population and educated researchers, and projects a sharp rise in available brainpower once computers reach human-brain capacity.

time.note: Date header as preserved in the relay (23 May 94 03:51:48 GMT, sci.nanotech); the relay lacks the Message-ID and transport headers, so the posting is not independently authenticated.

qualification: A hardware projection; computing throughput is not shown to equal intelligence. The wording is attested from 1997.

attested.note: Known only from the relay on Anders Sandberg’s web pages, captured by the Internet Archive on 1997-07-12.

thought.missing: Population, educated researchers and technology reinforce each other, and computer capacity rises with hardware trends; no machine improves its own intelligence or design capacity.

subject: extropy-1991-futique-neologisms
statement: The 1991 Extropy glossary defines singularity as a future point or period in which self-directed evolution accelerates through nanotechnology, neuroscience and AI, beyond which events cannot be reliably foreseen.

time.note: Winter/Spring 1991 on the page footer; the cover says Spring 1991.

qualification: The entry is credited to Vernor Vinge with the year 1986; that credit is the compiler’s attribution and does not date the checked wording. The compiler invites corrections.

thought.missing: Self-directed evolution accelerates broadly, without machine intelligence improving its own research capacity.

subject: good-1965
statement: Good’s chapter argues that an ultraintelligent machine, surpassing people at every intellectual activity including the design of machines, could design still better machines, so that there would be an "intelligence explosion" leaving human intelligence far behind.

time.note: Year of Advances in Computers, volume 6, as catalogued by Open Library; the current Crossref record gives 1966. The discrepancy is unresolved.

qualification: The chapter gives no timescale and says nothing about concealment. For the explosion it cites its references [22], [34] and [44]: Good’s 1951 review of a book by D. R. Hartree, an IBM report of 1959 (RC-115) and "The social implications of artificial intelligence" in The Scientist Speculates (1963); none was retrieved. An Internet Archive full-text search for the phrase in items indexed before 1965 found only unresolved or misdated hits.

claimed.note: The chapter’s footnote on p. 31 names talks in October 1962 and January 1963, a first draft of April 1963 and a slightly emended version of May 1964. None was retrieved, so the wording is not dated to them.

subject: extropians-1998-09-24-hanson
statement: Hanson’s reply of 1998-09-24 to Yudkowsky says there has long been positive feedback, and that neither feedback nor the ability to redesign AI architectures obviously suggests a break with history.

time.note: Sent header: Thu, 24 Sep 1998 09:51:22 -0700 (sender-local date).

qualification: It contests the inference, not the possibility of faster growth.

engagement.rationale: Gives a reason against the premise that positive feedback and the ability to redesign AI architectures imply a runaway: both have existed for a long time without a break with history.

thought.qualifier: Contests the inference from feedback to a break with history.

subject: iem-2013
statement: Intelligence Explosion Microeconomics identifies the key issue as returns on cognitive reinvestment: the ability to turn more computing power, faster computers or better algorithms into cognitive labour that produces larger or faster brains or better mind designs.

time.note: The report states "Last modified September 13, 2013".

qualification: Sets out "fizzle", moderate and intelligence-explosion regimes and attributes the moderate view to Hanson, which Hanson did not confirm. The fullest treatment located; an editorial judgement.

subject: moravec-1979-todays-computers

time.note: Issue of Analog (99, no. 2) given in the author’s publication list.

qualification: The compounding brings capable systems sooner; it does not describe a runaway beyond human level.

attested.note: Author-hosted HTML; the earliest Internet Archive capture, of 2001-07-10, is byte-identical to the copy retrieved in 2026. Not compared with the Analog pages.

thought.qualifier: Compounding improvement through machine labour in research.

subject: more-1998-singularity-meets-economy

thought.qualifier: Doubts an immediate explosion and a total transformation.

subject: solomonoff-1985-time-scale

subject: turing-c1951-heretical-theory

thought.missing: Machines sharpen their wits by conversing with each other; no design or research feedback is stated.

The quoted sentence continues 'but if there is one I suppose the Singularity is the best way to serve it', and the same message says 'any garden-variety superintelligence should be able to handle' figuring out the meaning of life, so he did not yet reject the premise that a sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true morality and be bound to act on it; that came in late 2000 (his SL4 message of 2000-11-13).
